Eva volunteers at her church every Saturday.
The church has a food drive this month.
People bring canned food to the pantry.
Dan stacks the pasta on a long shelf.
Eva has collected five boxes of donations.
Everyone pitches in for the charity.
Hi, Dan. How long have you volunteered at this church?

Since January. I drop by every Saturday.

Good idea. I brought a brochure from the charity too.

Sure. Everyone should pitch in today.

Today is the city marathon, and Ivan is at the finish line.
He has just crossed it after four hours.
He started at nine o'clock this morning.
He has a blister, a cramp, and a lot of sweat on his jersey.
His coworker Jo hands him some water.
He is thirsty and out of breath, but he ran for a charity.
Ivan, you did it! When did you cross the finish line?
At one o'clock. I have just sat down, and my legs hurt.
Have you had any water yet? Let me give you mine.
Thanks! I drank three cups on the road, but I'm still thirsty.
How are your feet? Did you get a blister?
Yes, I did. I've had one since the tenth mile.

At nine o'clock, the train was leaving the railway station.
Sara was sitting in the first carriage.
She was reading about a marathon.
Paul was looking at the timetable.
A man next to them was snoring.
Outside, goats were eating grass, and the scenery was beautiful.
Paul, did you hear the announcement? The train is stuck.
No, I didn't. I was looking at the timetable. What happened?
There is a problem on the railway. The conductor is talking to the driver now.
Oh no. I was reading about a marathon, so I didn't notice anything.
I was texting my coworker, but my phone has no signal.
Mine, too. I have canned food in my bag, so we can wait.
Look, the conductor is coming. Let's ask him together.
Good idea. I'm sure everyone on board wants to know.
Last night, Nora was cooking dinner at eight o'clock.
Suddenly, there was a blackout in the whole street.
It was dark, and Carl wasn't watching TV anymore.
They weren't scared, so they took out two glow sticks.
The ice cream in the fridge was starting to melt.
Then a gentle neighbor checked the fuse and started his generator.
Carl, the outage last night was long! Where were you?
I was at home. I was cooking pasta when the lights went out.
Oh no! Weren't you scared in the dark?
Not really. I had two glow sticks. What were you doing?
I was at the office with my coworker. The generator started after ten minutes.
Lucky you! My ice cream began to melt, and the milk could spoil.
But you have canned food in the pantry, right?
Yes, we do. We ate canned soup by candlelight, and it was fun.
Zoe was standing at the crossing near the railway.
While she was standing there, a red car was backing up.
A pedestrian was walking behind it, so the driver stopped.
The truck driver was honking while the car touched his bumper.
There was a scratch on the truck and a dent on the car.
Zoe was the only witness.
Thanks for waiting, ma'am. You're the witness, right?
Yes. I saw everything from the crossing near the railway.
Good. The lights were dark after the outage, right? What was the red car doing?
While I was waiting, the red car was backing up.
Was anyone walking behind it?
Yes, a pedestrian in a marathon shirt was crossing while the truck driver was honking.
I see. The red car has a dent, and the truck has a scratch. Did they pull over?
Yes, they both did. They're going to call their insurance today.
Last night, Nora was walking home from the park.
Suddenly, thunder shook the sky.
Lightning lit up the whole street.
Nora ran to a small café to take cover.
She left her wet umbrella in the umbrella stand.
She was soaked, and she began to shiver.
Hi! Can I wait here? I'm soaked, and I have mud on my raincoat.
Of course. Come in and put your umbrella in the umbrella stand.
Thanks. I was walking home from the park when the storm started.
Really? I was making coffee when I heard the thunder. It was so loud!
I think the whole town heard it. Is the power still on?
Not now. The blackout began ten minutes ago, but the generator works.
Great. A hot chocolate sounds cozy. Do you have one?
Sure! Each cup helps a charity, and I'm going to bring a blanket.
I was cooking dinner when the smoke detector started to beep.
I didn't panic, and I grabbed the extinguisher from the kitchen.
My neighbors were walking down the staircase when I opened the door.
A little boy was screaming on the stairs, but his mom stayed calm.
Smoke was rising to the ceiling when the firefighters arrived.
We escaped through the emergency exit, and nobody got hurt.
Ana, what were you doing when the alarm rang last night?
I was taking a shower when I heard the smoke detector.
Really? Did you panic?
A little. I put on my jacket and ran to the stairs with my neighbors.
We had to evacuate the whole building at midnight, and the siren was very loud.
Was it a real fire, or just a drill?
Just burnt popcorn on the third floor. A man was screaming at his microwave!
Ha! The blackout last month was worse, because the generator didn't start.
I remember. Were you walking down the staircase when the lights went out?
Yes, I was. I held a glow stick all the way down.
My grandparents live in a small house with a big porch.
My grandmother used to make a quilt every winter.
She has many wrinkles, but her smile is young.
My grandfather used to walk to school by the old railway.
He needs a cane now, but he still tells funny stories.
Every generation has a tradition, and ours is storytime on the porch.
Tom, did your grandparents grow up in this town?
Yes, they did. My grandfather used to work at the railway station.
Really? What did he do there?
He checked the timetable every morning and waved to each carriage.
That sounds great. My grandma used to be afraid of thunder and lightning.
Lots of kids are afraid of that. Did she hide under the bed?
Yes! She used to sit on the porch with a candle until the storm ended.
I love old stories. Now my grandfather writes everything in his diary.
Can I visit on Sunday and listen to his stories?
Sure, you can. He loves new listeners!
Back in the day, people didn't use cell phones every minute.
My dad used to call his friends on a landline.
He didn't use to send a text, so he went to a pay phone.
My mom used to listen to music on a cassette.
Her earphones were big and heavy.
My grandparents used to write on a typewriter, and they sent mail every week.
Leo, did you use to have a cell phone when you were ten?
No, I didn't. We only had a landline in the kitchen.
Wow. How did you talk to your friends?
We used a pay phone near school, and we sent a lot of mail.
That sounds hard. Did people use to take photos with film?
Yes, they did. We waited a week to see the pictures.
A week? My grandparents say the same, but my generation gets everything in one second.
True. I didn't use to listen to music on my phone. I had a big cassette player.
I love that. Back in the day, life was slower, right?
Yes, it was. I'm glad I got to grow up that way.
Mia is in a store, and she needs a new tablet.
The store assistant shows her three different models.
This brand is cheap, but the screen is small.
The other tablet is a good deal, and it comes with a stylus and a charger.
Mia asks, "Is it in stock?" and the assistant says yes.
The warranty is two years, so Mia smiles and says, "I'll take it."
Mia, are you buying a new gadget today, or just looking?
I'm buying a tablet. My grandparents gave me my old one, and it's broken.
Look at this one. It's lighter than a typewriter, and the price is only 200 dollars.
Hmm, the screen is nice. Does it have a warranty?
Let me ask the store assistant. Excuse me, does this tablet come with a charger?

Great! Buy a case too. Back in the day, people had no cases, and phones broke all the time.
True. I'll get a blue case, and I'll pay with my card.
And I'll carry the bag, because I'm your best friend, right?
Yes, you are, Dan. Thanks for the help.
The weather forecast says tomorrow will be cloudy.
In the morning, there will be fog and a light drizzle.
The humidity will be high, and the temperature will be chilly.
A cool breeze will come from the sea in the afternoon.
At night, hail will fall in the north, and it will be freezing.
By Sunday, the sky will clear up, and the sun will shine.
Ben, did you see the forecast on your tablet?
Yes, I did. It will rain all day tomorrow, and there will be thunder.
Oh no! I was going to wash my car.
Don't worry. Sunday will be sunny.
Really? The last forecast was wrong. It said lightning on Friday, and we had only a drizzle.
I remember. Everybody ran to take cover under the bus stop.
Ha! This time I'll bring an umbrella just in case.
Smart. Keep it near the umbrella stand, and don't forget it.
Thanks! By the way, is the temperature going to drop tonight?
Yes, it is. It's going to be freezing, so wear a jacket.
Lia and Noah are going to spend a week at the beach.
Lia is going to buy sunscreen, because she doesn't want a sunburn.
Noah is going to bring a cooler with cold drinks.
At the beach, a lifeguard sits near the water.
Noah wants a tan, so Lia says, "I'll bring a hat for you."
The kids are going to build a sandcastle, and the adults are going to rest.
Noah, are you ready for the beach trip? You should pack your bags tonight.
I'm going to pack after dinner. I already have my flip-flops and a hat.
Great. Oh no, I forgot the sunscreen! I'll buy some on the way.
Good idea. I want to bring a snorkel because I love to dive near the rocks.
Cool! The lifeguard says the water is clear, and a pelican lives there.
Wait, the hotel is calling me. Hold on, I'll answer it.
Okay. Ask about the weather. Is there humidity, or just a nice breeze?
They say it's sunny now, and the clouds clear up by noon.
Perfect. I'm so excited! Did you bring a cooler for the drinks?
Yes, I did. It's in the car, and the sandcastle bucket is there too.
It's December 31, and Nina has a big resolution.
She is on a diet, so she won't eat cake tonight.
Her brother Noah says, "I won't be lazy this year."
He wants to save money, so he made a budget.

They write their goals on paper, and they promise to stick to them all year.
Noah, what is your resolution for this year?
I won't waste money anymore. I want to save for a trip.
Good plan. Did you make a budget on your tablet?
Yes, I did. And I won't buy another gadget this year.
That's hard! Last year, you wanted to quit snacks, and then you ate a whole pie.

Okay. My resolution is to be less lazy. I'm going to run every morning.
Run in flip-flops? Please buy real shoes first!
Ha, I already have shoes. I only need to stick to my plan.
Yes, you can do it. Together we can stick to our goals.
It's Saturday morning, and the weather is great.
Eva and Jack have a picnic basket, a hammock, and a trail map.
Jack says, "Let's hike to the lake today."
Eva asks, "Shall we camp there tonight?"

At the campsite, a pelican watches them, and a nice breeze comes from the lake.
Jack, what are we doing this weekend? The weather is perfect.
Let's go to the lake. We can hike and have a picnic there.
Sounds fun! Shall we take the hammock too?

Right. After the hike, let's camp at the campsite near the river.
Good. The kids can skate on the path while we rest.
The sky is cloudy now, but it should clear up soon, and I'll bring a thermos with hot tea.
Yes, I think so. Pack the thermos, and we're ready to go!
Ruth was driving near an intersection when a traffic cop stopped her.

Ruth, why are you late? Did you have a parking problem?

Sounds fun! I have the picnic basket in the trunk, and the trail map is here.
Great. But look, a big car is blocking us, and the tow truck is coming!
Don't worry, it's someone else's car. Yes, we can go now!

She is going to rent a small house near the beach.

Ana has been running every morning for a month.

Okay, Mia. Everything is fine, and I'm ready for the next test.

Lia has a cold today, but she has to work from home.

Mia and Ben go to a small Chinese restaurant.

Noah is in an electronics store.
He needs new earbuds for his phone.
The tag says they are on sale today.

Mia checks the school canteen menu today.
The fried dumplings have the most calories on the menu.
The baked fish has less salt and more protein.
The beans have the least calories and a lot of fiber.

She buys beans, nuts, and a small pasta.
Hi, Ben. What are you getting for lunch today?

Sure, the baked fish has less salt and more protein than the dumplings.

Yes, you can. And take a drink with less sugar than a soda.

Rosa and Noah visit the farmers market on Saturday.
The peaches are in season, so they smell great.
A seller offers a sample of organic melon on a toothpick.
Rosa has to pay in cash because the stand has no card machine.
Noah must carry the heavy bags.
If it rains, they will go home early.
Wow, this market is huge. What do you want to buy first?
We should buy the peaches. They're in season, and they're on sale.
Good idea. Look, there's a sample of melon here. Help yourself!
Mmm, this plum is sweet. Is it organic? Let me ask.

Yes, I have two big ones. We can put them in the car.
Great. I want to cut down on cookies, so I'm buying pears, spinach, and herbs.
Smart. After that, let's order two coffees at the stand and sit down.
Sure, let's go.
Ana is at the street market with her brother Ben.
The butcher has good meat, but his price tag is a lot higher than at the store.
Organic melons are in season, but they cost far more here, and Ana says it's a rip-off.
Ben likes to haggle, so he asks the man to weigh a dozen coconuts again.
The man gives them a sample of the melon, and it's much sweeter than the last one.
Ana laughs because the deal is far better than before.
Excuse me, sir. The price on this melon is a lot higher than yesterday.
Really? Melons are much more expensive this week, ma'am.
The butcher next door is much cheaper. Honestly, this looks like a rip-off.
Hold on! Let me weigh it again. Maybe the price tag is wrong.
Okay. Can you give me a better price for the melon and a dozen coconuts?
Hmm. I like to haggle, so tell me your price.
Eight dollars for the melon and the coconuts. Is that okay?
Deal! Eight dollars. Thanks for coming to my stall.
Lia and Noah are looking at photos from their trip.
The canyon is the most beautiful place Lia has ever seen.
They took the photo at sunrise with a new camera lens.
Their itinerary had a famous landmark, but they chose a road off the beaten path.
At the lodge, a friendly traveler showed them a map in her guidebook.
It was the best trip they have ever taken.
Look at this photo! The canyon is the most beautiful place I've ever seen.
Wow, that's amazing. Did you use the new camera lens?
Yes! I took it at sunrise. It's the best photo I've ever taken.
Our itinerary was great, but the landmark was very crowded, and lunch was a rip-off.
That's true. I liked the lodge off the beaten path much more.
Same here. And the organic breakfast was delicious, wasn't it?
It really was. The traveler at the lodge gave us that tip, remember?
Of course I do! Let's go again next summer.
Rosa is in a hurry because the meeting starts at nine.
It is rush hour, and a long traffic jam fills the street.
Drivers honk their horns, but nobody moves.
Rosa leaves the cab, crosses at the crosswalk, and runs to the station.
She swipes her card at the turnstile, and the monthly fee is already paid.
An announcement says the train is late, so the more she waits, the angrier she feels.
Tom! Why are you running? The meeting starts at nine thirty.
I know, but the traffic jam was terrible. I left my cab on Main Street.
Come on, hurry up. The turnstile is on the left.
Done. Is the train late again?
Yes. The earlier you leave home, the easier the trip is.
You're right. The more I wait, the more nervous I feel.
Relax. We can read my itinerary and the guidebook while we wait.
Sure. Let's do it, and I'll buy the coffee.
Mia is on the subway at rush hour, and the crowd is huge.
The train is packed like sardines, and the air is stuffy.
There are too many people and too much noise in the car.
A baby in a stroller cries, and a man bumps into Mia.
The chatter is loud, and the noise level only goes up.
At the turnstile, a long queue of sweaty people waits to leave.
Ben, this train is packed like sardines. I can't breathe!
I know. There are too many people, and the air is stuffy.

Sorry about that! There's too much noise, and nobody listens.
The traffic jam above ground is bad, so everyone takes the subway.

Good plan. Tomorrow I'll leave an hour earlier. Too much stress is bad for me.
Deal. See you at the turnstile at seven.
Noah and Rosa are cooking dinner for twelve people.
They have organic peaches, but they don't have enough for everyone.
Rosa counts every ingredient on the counter.
Noah pours water into the pot and uses a whisk to mix the sauce.
The colander is big enough, but the skillet isn't big enough for all the vegetables.

Do we have enough rice for twelve people?

Sure. Did you buy the peaches? They're in season now.
Yes, but only six. That's not enough for dessert.
No problem. Six peaches and some ice cream. I'll be back soon.
Lia and Tom have a lemonade stand in front of their house.
Lia squeezes ten lemons into a big pitcher.
The lemonade is too sour, so Tom adds sugar from the measuring cup.
Then he puts in some ice cubes, some mint, and one berry in each glass.
A long queue forms, and the lemonade is cold enough now.
Lia sprinkles sugar on top and slices a lime for each cup.
Taste this. Is it sweet enough, or is it too sour?
It's too sour! Our best ingredient is sugar, so add more.

Sure. Wait, my hands are sticky from the flour.
Wash them, then squeeze two more limes. We need a bigger batch.
Done! Now it's sweet enough. Customers are in the queue already.
Great! Add some ice cubes, and the drink will be cold enough.
Okay, ice cubes in now. We're ready to open!
Ana makes breakfast for Noah on Sunday morning.
She pours a little milk from the carton into his coffee.
Then she adds a teaspoon of sugar and a pinch of cinnamon.
On the table there are a few bagels, and a crumb falls on the floor.
Noah eats a bowl of oats with a spoonful of honey.
Ana squeezes a little orange juice into a pitcher with a few ice cubes.
Do you want some milk in your coffee, Noah?
Yes, just a little, please. I don't like it too white.
Okay. Do you want sugar? I only have a little left.
Just a teaspoon, and add a pinch of nutmeg if you have it.
Sure. I have a few bagels with cheese. Do you want one?
Yes, please. Oh no, there are a few crumbs on your shirt!

Mia and Tom went to the store and bought food in bulk.

Now the pantry has lots of pasta, and there is plenty of rice.
Mia puts a sack of lentils on the shelf and the granola in a jar.

Tom just smiles because they have lots of tortillas for the whole month.
Look at our pantry! We have lots of pasta and rice now.
Yes, we bought them in bulk. There's plenty of room on the shelf.
Check the date on the cereal box. What's the shelf life?

Good. Did you wait in the queue long at the store?
No, I went before the rush hour. It took just ten minutes.
Perfect. I need a teaspoon of salt for the soup. Is there any left?
Yes, it's in the jar next to the granola.
Ben lives in an apartment with a small balcony and a long corridor.
He has a neighbor who stomps and thumps all night.

He talks to the landlady, a woman who lives on the first floor.

Tomorrow the neighbor must keep it down, or Ben will leave a note on his doormat.

Thanks, but first I'll leave a note on his doormat: please keep it down.

Ana and Noah spend Saturday at the mall.

At the checkout, the clerk puts everything in a shopping bag.

Ben's garage, which has a long workbench, is full of tools.

Ben, do you have a tape measure? I can't find mine.

Lia and her son Noah go to a pet shop near the park.

Ana loves the paperback she bought at the clearance table.

In a bakery, the dough is kneaded by hand and left to rise.

Today he stops at the gym to work out.

Ana's desk is a mess this morning.
